Taste more. Waste less.

THE PROBLEM WE’RE CRACKING

Food Left Behind.
Resources Lost with It.

An unsold sandwich represents more than the food in the case. Growing its ingredients takes land and water; preparing, refrigerating, and delivering it takes energy and people’s work. When food goes uneaten, those resources have already been used.

Much of food waste’s climate impact happens before disposal, through production, processing, and transport. Preventing waste can protect the value of those resources. Why Food Waste Matters ↗

MarketBite starts with a practical campus opportunity: connect surplus inventory to timely, responsible price drops so more prepared food finds a buyer. Our goal is less unsold food and more affordable meals. A future pilot would compare unsold quantities and discarded food against a baseline, alongside student savings and cafe revenue.

THE PEOPLE BEHIND MARKETBITE

Built at Rochester.

Campus food waste felt close to home. As University of Rochester students, we saw an opportunity to help the cafes we visit every day sell more of their prepared food while making meals more affordable.

Our inspiration came from stock market bars, where drink prices rise and fall with customer demand and live screens help guests spot a deal. We adapted that concept for campus dining: prices respond to remaining inventory and time, while alerts encourage students to purchase surplus before it goes to waste.

Over the ten-day Ain Center’s The Heist Hackathon, we brought together product design, software development, business strategy, and sustainability research to build MarketBite. Competing in the Sustainability track, we chose Connections Cafe as the setting for our prototype.

Looking ahead, we hope to bring MarketBite to college campuses, independent cafes, and small food businesses across the United States. Starting with a campus pilot would help us learn what works and adapt the platform to different menus, customer habits, and operating needs.

REDUCING CARBON EMISSIONS

Less Waste. Less Wasted Energy.

Food carries a footprint from farming, processing, refrigeration, and transport. When food decomposes in a landfill, it can also generate methane. Preventing waste can reduce those emissions over time.

Our aim is to get more prepared food eaten and help cafes plan future stock more accurately. Price drops give students an incentive to buy surplus; the inventory record shows what is still left behind.

FROM SIMULATION TO IMPACT

Measure the Food. Then the Footprint.

This simulator tracks surplus purchases and food left at close. In a campus pilot, we would weigh unsold and discarded food, compare it with similar days without MarketBite, and use food-specific emissions factors to estimate the carbon reduction.

Sales show how food moves. Confirming waste and emissions prevented requires that comparison; retained or transferred food is tracked separately.

Food & TickerOn MenuOpening StockRegular Price ($)Minimum ($)Sale Cost ($)
Add a Food
03: Pricing Rules

Choose how often prices are reviewed and how far they may change. The minimum prices and sale costs from step 2 still apply. Include any selling fees and the minimum amount you want to keep per item after those costs.

Choose 5-, 30-, or 60-minute reviews; the default is 30 simulated minutes. The default discount cap is 45%. Ordinary changes use up to 5% of the regular price, rounded up to cents; a higher price floor takes priority. Prices never exceed the regular price. New orders stop five minutes before each batch’s deadline.

How the Pricing Model Works

The Food Display, Exchange Display, and Mobile Display use the same confirmed prices. The target discount equals the chosen discount cap × the share of starting stock still available × the share of the selling window already elapsed. Reserved and set-aside items are excluded from available stock.

At the default 45% cap, a $10 item with half its stock available halfway through its window has an unrounded target discount of 11.25%. Rounding the $8.875 target upward gives $8.88, or 11.2% off. Starting at $10, the default 50-cent step confirms $9.50 at that review: the displayed discount is 5%, provided no higher floor applies.

The floor is the greatest of one cent, the owner’s minimum, the discount-cap minimum, and (sale cost + allocated fee + required contribution) ÷ (1 − percentage fee). It covers the entered assumptions, not the cafe’s total costs or guaranteed profit. An offer pauses if its floor exceeds the regular price.

Lower stock can raise prices even near closing. With one of 20 items left, six minutes remaining in a 120-minute window, and a $10 regular price, the default target is $9.79 before any higher floor. This model balances remaining stock with time; it does not guarantee a closing clearance discount.

Purchases update stock immediately; automatic price changes wait for the next scheduled review. Counts more than 30 minutes old pause offers. More frequent reviews allow more steps toward the target without changing the formula or freshness limit.

04: Customer Traffic & Rushes

Set normal hourly purchases in person and through mobile orders. Then choose rush times, durations, and multipliers. A 2× rush doubles both rates; actual purchases depend on available stock.

05: Scheduled Offers

Choose a Food Bundle or Market Crash, then set its time and duration. Bundles combine two foods at their current prices; a Market Crash highlights eligible price drops within your rules. Apply Deal saves the offer for the simulation and all menus. Use Launch Now only when you want to run it immediately.

    MARKETBITE ALERTS

    Good Deals.
    Right on Time.

    A timely deal can turn a passing thought into a cafe visit. MarketBite alerts encourage students to stop by and buy surplus food at a lower price before it goes to waste.

    Follow the Price

    Price-drop and Closing Rush notifications point students to current offers. The menu updates with the same prices and availability, so students can check the deal before heading over.

    A Better Bite. Less Left Behind.

    For students, it’s a more affordable bite. For cafes, it’s a chance to sell food that might otherwise be left behind—and make better use of the water, energy, and work that went into it.
